name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q01 - Sequence for building cubic close packed structure

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages in the correct logical sequence to build a three-dimensional cubic close-packed (ccp) structure from identical hard spheres:

  • P. Placing a second hexagonal close-packed layer into the depressions of the first layer to generate tetrahedral and octahedral voids.
  • Q. Arranging spheres in a single row touching each other in one dimension.
  • R. Placing a third layer over the octahedral voids of the second layer, followed by a fourth layer aligned with the first layer.
  • S. Stacking rows in a staggered manner to form a two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layer.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A three-dimensional close-packed crystal lattice is constructed step by step from one-dimensional rows to two-dimensional layers and finally to three-dimensional stacking.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Stage
First, spheres are arranged in a single one-dimensional row touching each other.
Second, additional rows are placed in a staggered manner in the depressions of the first row to form a two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layer.
Third, a second hexagonal close-packed layer is placed into the depressions of the first layer, creating both tetrahedral and octahedral voids.
Fourth, to obtain a cubic close-packed (ccp) \(\text{ABCABC}\ldots\) arrangement rather than hexagonal close packing, the third layer is placed to cover the octahedral voids of the second layer, and the fourth layer aligns with the first layer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical sequence is one-dimensional row formation \(\to\) two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layer \(\to\) second layer creating tetrahedral and octahedral voids \(\to\) third layer covering octahedral voids with fourth layer aligned with the first.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q02 - Sequence of F centre formation in sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order when a crystal of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is heated in an atmosphere of sodium vapour to develop a yellow colour:

  • P. Diffusion of released electrons into the crystal to occupy anionic vacancies (F-centres).
  • Q. Deposition of sodium atoms on the surface of the \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) crystal.
  • R. Excitation of unpaired electrons at anionic sites by absorbing energy from visible light.
  • S. Diffusion of \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions to the surface to combine with \(\mathrm{Na}\) atoms, accompanied by loss of electrons from \(\mathrm{Na}\) atoms to form \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heating an alkali halide crystal in the vapour of its alkali metal produces a metal excess defect due to anionic vacancies, known as F-centres, which impart colour to the crystal.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Event
Initially, sodium atoms from the vapour deposit on the surface of the \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) crystal.
Next, \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions diffuse to the crystal surface and combine with the deposited \(\mathrm{Na}\) atoms to form \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), while the sodium atoms lose electrons to form \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions.
Then, the released electrons diffuse inward into the crystal and occupy the vacant anionic sites, forming F-centres.
Finally, when visible light falls on the crystal, these unpaired electrons absorb energy and get excited, imparting a yellow colour to \(\mathrm{NaCl}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is surface deposition of \(\mathrm{Na}\) atoms \(\to\) outward diffusion of \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions and electron loss by \(\mathrm{Na}\) \(\to\) inward diffusion of electrons into anionic sites \(\to\) absorption of visible light by unpaired electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q03 - Increasing order of electrical conductivity in solids

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following classes of solids in increasing order of their typical electrical conductivity:

  • P. Metallic conductors
  • Q. Insulators
  • R. Doped extrinsic semiconductors
  • S. Pure intrinsic semiconductors

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical conductivity of solids spans \(27\) orders of magnitude from \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{7}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\), governed by the energy gap between the valence band and conduction band and the concentration of charge carriers.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Class
Insulators have a large forbidden energy gap and the lowest conductivity (\(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{-10}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\)).
Pure intrinsic semiconductors have a small energy gap, giving intermediate conductivity (\(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{4}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\)), which is too low for most practical uses.
Doping an intrinsic semiconductor with electron-rich or electron-deficient impurities increases the charge carrier concentration and raises its conductivity above that of the pure intrinsic semiconductor.
Metallic conductors have overlapping or partially filled bands and exhibit the highest conductivity (\(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of electrical conductivity is insulators \(<\) pure intrinsic semiconductors \(<\) doped extrinsic semiconductors \(<\) metallic conductors.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q04 - Sequence of steps to calculate molar mass from unit cell

questiontext.text:
To determine the molar mass \(M\) of an unknown metal crystallising in a cubic unit cell of known edge length \(a\), density \(d\), and number of atoms per unit cell \(z\), arrange the calculation steps in the correct logical sequence:

  • P. Multiply the mass of a single atom \(m\) by the Avogadro constant \(N_A\) to obtain the molar mass \(M\).
  • Q. Calculate the mass of one unit cell by multiplying the density \(d\) by the unit cell volume \(a^3\).
  • R. Divide the mass of one unit cell by \(z\) to obtain the mass of a single atom \(m\).
  • S. Determine the volume of one cubic unit cell as \(a^3\) from the edge length \(a\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The known quantities for the cubic crystal are edge length \(a\), density \(d\), number of atoms per unit cell \(z\), and Avogadro constant \(N_A\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The density of a single unit cell equals the bulk density \(d\) of the crystalline solid.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Unit cell volume \(V = a^3\); mass of unit cell \(= d \cdot a^3 = z \cdot m\); molar mass \(M = m \cdot N_A\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, compute the volume of the cubic unit cell as \(V = a^3\).
Second, multiply this volume by the density \(d\) to find the total mass of the unit cell, \(d \cdot a^3\).
Third, divide the unit cell mass by \(z\) (the number of atoms in one unit cell) to obtain the mass of one atom, \(m = \frac{d a^3}{z}\).
Fourth, multiply \(m\) by \(N_A\) to get the molar mass, \(M = \frac{d a^3 N_A}{z}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units simplify as \(\frac{(\text{g cm}^{-3})(\text{cm}^3)(\text{mol}^{-1})}{1} = \text{g mol}^{-1}\). Thus, the correct sequence is computing \(a^3\) \(\to\) computing unit cell mass \(d a^3\) \(\to\) dividing by \(z\) for single-atom mass \(m\) \(\to\) multiplying by \(N_A\) for molar mass \(M\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q05 - Sequence of derivation for bcc packing efficiency

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following geometric steps in the correct logical order to derive the packing efficiency (\(68\%\)) of a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell of edge length \(a\) and atomic radius \(r\):

  • P. Equate the body diagonal to \(4r\) to obtain \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\).
  • Q. Apply the Pythagorean theorem on a cube face to find the face diagonal \(b = \sqrt{2}a\).
  • R. Divide the volume of \(2\) spheres by the cube volume \(a^3 = \left(\frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3\) and multiply by \(100\%\).
  • S. Apply the Pythagorean theorem using an edge and the face diagonal to find the body diagonal \(c = \sqrt{3}a\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A body-centred cubic unit cell has edge length \(a\), atomic radius \(r\), and \(z = 2\) atoms per unit cell.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a bcc unit cell, the atom at the body centre touches two corner atoms along the body diagonal, so the body diagonal length equals \(4r\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Pythagorean theorem in right triangles and volume of a sphere \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, find the face diagonal \(b\) from two perpendicular cube edges: \(b^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2 \implies b = \sqrt{2}a\).
Second, find the body diagonal \(c\) from an edge and the face diagonal: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = a^2 + 2a^2 = 3a^2 \implies c = \sqrt{3}a\).
Third, equate the body diagonal to \(4r\): \(\sqrt{3}a = 4r \implies a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\).
Fourth, compute the packing efficiency: \(\frac{2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{\left(\frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8} \times 100\% = 68\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each step depends directly on the previous relation, giving the unique logical order: face diagonal \(b = \sqrt{2}a\) \(\to\) body diagonal \(c = \sqrt{3}a\) \(\to\) edge-radius relation \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\) \(\to\) ratio of sphere volume to cube volume times \(100\%\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q06 - Sequence of p type semiconductor conduction mechanism

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct sequence to explain electrical conduction in a \(p\)-type semiconductor formed from silicon:

  • P. Apparent movement of positively charged electron holes towards the negatively charged plate under an applied electric field.
  • Q. Doping pure silicon (group \(14\)) with a trace amount of a group \(13\) element such as boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) having three valence electrons.
  • R. Jumping of an electron from a neighbouring atom to fill the vacancy, leaving an electron hole at its original position.
  • S. Formation of three covalent bonds around the dopant atom and one electron-deficient site called an electron hole.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Pure silicon has four valence electrons per atom, forming four covalent bonds with its neighbours, and is doped with a group \(13\) impurity such as boron.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Under an external electric field, electrons move towards the positively charged plate, while electron vacancies (holes) appear to move in the opposite direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Doping with an electron-deficient group \(13\) element creates electronic defects (electron holes) that enable conduction.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, silicon (group \(14\)) is doped with a group \(13\) element like boron, which has three valence electrons.
Second, boron forms three complete covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms, leaving the fourth bond incomplete as an electron hole.
Third, an electron from a neighbouring silicon atom jumps to fill this hole, creating a new electron hole at its original site.
Fourth, under an applied electric field, as electrons move towards the positive plate through these holes, it appears as if positively charged holes are moving towards the negative plate.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The causal sequence is doping with group \(13\) element \(\to\) formation of an electron hole \(\to\) electron jumping from a neighbouring atom leaving a new hole \(\to\) apparent migration of positive holes towards the negative plate.
